**Where is the ball most likely going, and what would change your answer after the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**To X on the left, most likely a fade.** Everything about the alignment points there. X is alone on his side,
lined up with about 7 yards to the sideline, exactly the room a fade needs. The corner is pressing a yard
off him and lined up a step *inside* him: inside leverage, which takes away the slant and gives up the
outside release. And the safety help has rotated toward the three receivers on the right: the strong safety
has walked over them and the free safety sits in the end zone just outside the right hash, much too far away
to reach a ball thrown toward the left pylon a second after the snap. The three receivers on the right are
there partly to *pull* that help away. Coaches call this a "backside" or isolation fade.

**What would change it:** if the corner ran with X stride for stride over the top, the better throw is the
back-shoulder: thrown early, behind X's outside shoulder, and caught a yard or two deep in the end zone. If
the corner had lined up outside X, the slant would be open instead. And if the free safety had stayed in the
middle or shaded left, the quarterback would likely work the three-receiver side, where the defense would
then be short a man.
:::
:::

**You have the four shapes from the two-point figure (A–D) on your call sheet. Which one do you call
against this look, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**D, the quarterback run (QB power), with the sprint-out option (C) as the second choice.** Count the box:
four linemen and one linebacker, five defenders. Count your blockers on a quarterback run: five linemen
plus the running back, six, and the quarterback carries the ball. That is one more blocker than the box has
defenders, the extra-hat arithmetic, and the two safeties are standing three or four yards deep in the end
zone, so the runner needs only two yards before they arrive. The defense has bet everything on stopping a
pass: a defender on every receiver and two more behind them. The bunch rub (A) and the snag (B) would throw
into that bet.

**What would change it:** a safety walking down into the box before the snap (or, harder to see, timing his
run to arrive at the snap). Then the count is even and the pass becomes the better bet, because a defender
has left the coverage. That trade, the defense guessing and the offense counting, is the whole two-point
game. Most defenses avoid this look for exactly this reason: on the 2023–2025 two-point tries in the
participation data, they had six or seven defenders in the box on 71% of them.
:::
:::

**The defense has packed everyone in to stop the run. What call makes it pay, and which offensive player
should you watch?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Play-action from the same look.** The quarterback fakes the iso to the running back behind the fullback;
the line fires out exactly as it did on first down, so every defender's eyes go to the pile. Then a tight
end who seemed to be blocking slips into the end zone: Y or U blocks for a count and releases, or the wing,
H, leaks to the corner of the end zone. Watch **the backside tight end, U**. On a run he blocks the end in
front of him; on play-action he chips the end and releases, and the defensive back responsible for him,
crept up to help against the run, is the one who has to see it.

This is exactly what goal-line offenses do. Inside the 3 in 2023–2025, offenses with one wide receiver or
none passed on only 28% of snaps, but 66% of those passes came
off a run fake. **What could go wrong:** a defense in a 5-3 has an extra linebacker standing up who can see
the release, and a quarterback under center who fakes and turns his back has very little time against a
front built to get into the backfield. One more run is never a bad answer either; the threat of the pass is
what keeps those three defensive backs honest.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Near the goal line the **end line becomes the deepest defender**. The compressed field squeezes zones,
  frees safeties to come down, and makes man coverage, press and Cover 0 cheap. The offense loses its deep
  threat, and every throw arrives into a crowd.
- Red-zone pass concepts win quickly and close: the **fade** and **back-shoulder throw** against press with no
  outside help, the **slant** when the corner takes away the fade, **rubs** from stacks and bunches against
  man, the **shovel pass** against an attacking front, and the **sprint-out** that puts a flat defender in
  conflict.
- A good **two-point play** gives the offense two answers that put one defender in conflict, so it works
  against more than one defensive call. Runs have converted more often than passes since 2015, partly
  because of who chooses to run, and a try is worth about what the kick is, so the scoreboard decides.
- **Goal-line defenses** (6-2, 5-3) trade defensive backs for linemen and linebackers and fill every gap;
  low man wins. Their weakness is the play that looks like the run and isn't, which is why heavy personnel
  that throws near the goal line almost always fakes a run first.
- The **QB sneak** is the best one-yard play in football: the ball starts closest to the line, the play is
  instant, and the quarterback-as-runner adds a blocker. The **tush push** adds pushers behind him; it has
  been legal since the NFL removed the ban on pushing the runner in the **mid-2000s** (2005 or 2006; pulling is still a foul),
  survived a **22–10 ban vote in 2025**, and is legal in **2026**.
- In the data, a little under six red-zone trips in ten end in touchdowns; a first-and-goal from the 1 scores
  about nine times in ten (a drive gets four tries); and sneaks convert about four in five on 1 yard to go,
  but only about half the time on 2. Teams differ far more in how often they sneak than in how well, and the
  teams that sneak most face the hardest looks.
